screens.title: Organizing Complexity: Composite and Facade
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll study two complementary structural patterns that help you manage complexity in software. First, you will learn the Composite pattern, which lets you represent part‑whole hierarchies so clients call the same operations on single objects and on object collections. Think of files and directories: the same display or size calculation works whether you call it on a single file or on an entire directory tree. Second, you'll learn the Facade pattern, which creates a single, higher‑level interface to orchestrate many subsystem classes so a client performs a complex task with a single call. For example, a watch movie method can dim lights, start the projector, and set the amplifier without the client wiring all those calls together. Together these patterns let you reduce duplication, simplify client code, and keep subsystems decoupled. We'll walk concrete Python examples for each, point out common pitfalls such as bloated interfaces or hiding too much, and finish with a practical activity. Consider what large system you interact with daily that feels awkward to use; this lesson will give you two design tools to fix it.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about and implement two structural patterns that tame complexity. First, you will understand how to design a Component interface and separate Leaf and Composite implementations so that client code calls the same operations on a single object or an entire tree. You will practice this by modeling file system entries or organizational charts, implementing display and size calculations that recurse through children. Second, you will be able to design a Facade that hides complex orchestration behind a concise A P I. You will implement a home‑theater or DevOps pipeline facade that sequences multiple subsystem calls, and you will learn when a facade should expose or hide subsystem classes. Finally, you will learn to recognize pitfalls: do not put methods in the Component that only make sense for one role, and do not let a facade become a god object that duplicates subsystem functionality. These skills help you build modular, maintainable systems that are easier to test and adapt.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical skills and common pitfalls. You will implement Composite tree structures with working add and remove operations and a display behavior that recurses cleanly. Practice computing aggregated values like total size, and pay attention to interface design: only put methods in the shared Component interface that make sense for both leaves and composites. You will also implement a Facade that orchestrates multiple subsystem classes and exposes high‑level operations, such as watch or run pipeline. While writing facades, make clear decisions about which subsystem functionality to expose and when to allow clients to access the subsystem directly. A frequent mistake is making the facade do too much or, conversely, exposing every subsystem method again through the facade, which defeats simplification. By the end of the exercises you should be able to choose between exposing a facade, delegating specific calls, or leaving fine‑grained control to advanced clients.

screens.title: Composite vs Facade — What each solves
screens.narratorSegment: Let's contrast the two patterns by focusing on intent and client impact. The Composite pattern addresses the problem of uniformity: you want clients to treat single objects and recursive compositions the same way. The core of Composite is a shared Component interface plus leaf and composite implementations; common operations are implemented at both levels and composites delegate to their children. Use Composite when you have part‑whole hierarchies such as file systems, UI element trees, or organizational charts. A common misconception is that Composite is about simplifying subsystem complexity; instead, it focuses on uniformity of structure and recursion. Facade solves a different problem: an application must interact with a set of heterogeneous subsystem classes, and that interaction is complex. The Facade provides a higher‑level A P I that orchestrates subsystem calls. For example, a watch movie method sequences lights, projector, and player. A misconception is to confuse Facade with Adapter: an Adapter changes a single interface to match another, while Facade offers a new, simplified A P I that aggregates many interfaces. Finally, Decorator is sometimes confused with Composite; Decorator adds behavior to single objects, not to whole trees. Decide by asking: does the problem require uniform object composition or simplified orchestration of many classes?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Composite vs Facade
When to use Composite
Choose Composite for part‑whole hierarchies where you want recursive operations to behave identically on leaves and composites. Typical examples include file systems, UI element trees, and organizational charts.
  • Design a minimal Component interface with only shared operations.
  • Implement Leaf for terminal objects and Composite to manage children.
  • Watch out for adding methods that only apply to one role.
Misconception
Composite does not simplify subsystem orchestration; it normalizes object structures.
When to use Facade
Choose Facade when you need a single, convenient API for a complex set of classes. Use a Facade to reduce coupling and make common tasks easier to call from clients.
  • Let the Facade orchestrate subsystem calls for common workflows.
  • Keep the facade focused; allow direct subsystem access for advanced clients if needed.
  • Beware of turning a facade into a monolithic god object.
Pro tip
Name facade methods after meaningful client tasks, not after low‑level subsystem methods.

screens.title: Composite Pattern — Core structure
screens.narratorSegment: The Composite pattern models part‑whole hierarchies by defining three roles. First, the Component is an abstract interface or base class that declares the operations common to both individual items and compositions. Keep this interface minimal — include only methods that make sense for both leaves and composites. Second, the Leaf is a concrete object with no children that implements the Component interface. Leaves provide the fundamental behavior, like returning their own size or rendering themselves. Third, the Composite is a container that also implements Component and manages child components with add, remove, and get_children methods. When a composite receives an operation like display or get_size, it forwards that call to each child and aggregates the results. A concrete example is a directory: a directory lists itself and then iterates through children to display their entries; size is computed by summing child sizes. A common mistake is adding management or traversal-specific methods to Component that only composites need. Instead, place child management on Composite itself and keep the Component contract focused on shared operations. Understanding these roles helps you design clear, testable hierarchies.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Composite — Core
Component
Abstract interface for shared operations such as display and get_size. Keep it minimal.
Leaf
Concrete objects with no children. Implement shared operations returning their own data.
Composite
Containers that manage children and delegate operations to them, aggregating results.
Misconception
Do not place add/remove on the Component unless every component must support it. Prefer putting management methods on Composite.
Concrete example: File system
Files are leaves that report their own size. Directories are composites that sum child sizes and display structure recursively.
Python: component signatures
class FileSystemComponent:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def display(self, indent=""):
        raise NotImplementedError

    def get_size(self):
        raise NotImplementedError
Key Takeaway

Separate responsibilities: shared operations in Component; child management in Composite to avoid interface bloat.

screens.title: Composite — File system live code
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through a Python implementation that shows the Composite pattern in action. The example defines a FileSystemComponent base class with display and get_size methods. The File leaf stores its own size and prints its name and size when asked to display. The Directory composite keeps a list of children and implements add and remove. When display is called on a directory, it prints its heading and then calls display on each child, increasing the indentation. For get_size, the directory iterates through children and sums their sizes, returning the aggregate. A practical example: if you call get_size on the root directory, it returns the total of nested files even if they are many levels deep. Watch for an important design decision: child management methods are on Directory, not on File or the base component. A common learner mistake is to include traversal helpers in the base interface, which forces leaves to implement meaningless behavior. When testing, create a nested structure with files and directories, call display to verify formatting, and call get_size to confirm the sum. This demonstrates the recursive power of Composite and why clients can use a single interface for both leaves and compositions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Composite Code
File and Directory implementations
# Component
class FileSystemComponent:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def display(self, indent=""):
        raise NotImplementedError

    def get_size(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

# Leaf
class File(FileSystemComponent):
    def __init__(self, name, size):
        super().__init__(name)
        self._size = size

    def display(self, indent=""):
        print(f"{indent}- File: {self.name} ({self._size}KB)")

    def get_size(self):
        return self._size

# Composite
class Directory(FileSystemComponent):
    def __init__(self, name):
        super().__init__(name)
        self._children = []

    def add(self, component):
        self._children.append(component)

    def remove(self, component):
        self._children.remove(component)
Directory behavior
    def display(self, indent=""):
        print(f"{indent}+ Directory: {self.name}/")
        for child in self._children:
            child.display(indent + "  ")

    def get_size(self):
        total_size = 0
        for child in self._children:
            total_size += child.get_size()
        return total_size
Runtime example
Create a root directory, add files and nested directories, then call display and get_size to observe recursion and aggregation.
Key Takeaway

With Composite, a single client call can operate across many objects because composites delegate consistently to children.

Common Mistake
Avoid forcing leaves to implement add/remove or traversal methods that only composites need.

screens.title: Facade Pattern — Intent and structure
screens.narratorSegment: The Facade pattern provides a single, higher‑level interface to a collection of subsystem classes so clients can complete a common task without coordinating many low‑level calls. The Facade encapsulates the orchestration logic and delegates work to subsystem classes internally. The facade itself should not contain the core subsystem behavior; it directs where work is done. For example, a home theater facade might call lights, projector, amplifier, and player methods in sequence when asked to watch a movie. This hides the orchestration details and reduces coupling between the client and the subsystem. Remember that a facade is an optional convenience; clients that need fine‑grained control can still access subsystem classes directly. A common misconception is that a facade replaces unit testing for subsystem classes; you still test subsystems individually and test the facade for orchestration. Use facades to reduce repetitive wiring code and to provide a stable entry point to a changing subsystem implementation. Facade Pattern — Intent and structure means facade orchestrates multiple classes to provide a simple api for common client tasks while keeping subsystems testable and accessible.. In practical terms, simplify client interaction with a complex subsystem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Facade — Core
Roles
Facade: a single class exposing high‑level methods. Subsystem classes: the components the facade delegates to. Clients: call the facade for common tasks and optionally interact directly with subsystems when needed.
Design guidance: name facade methods for whole tasks, keep orchestration in the facade, and avoid re‑exposing every subsystem method unless necessary.
Why it matters
Facades reduce client complexity and help maintain a stable API when subsystems evolve.
Example: Home Theater
A watch_movie method dims lights, powers projector, configures amplifier, and starts the player. The client calls one method, the facade handles the sequence.
Facade snippet
class HomeTheaterFacade:
    def __init__(self, projector, amplifier, bluray, lights):
        self._projector = projector
        self._amplifier = amplifier
        self._bluray = bluray
        self._lights = lights

    def watch_movie(self, movie_title):
        self._lights.dim(10)
        self._projector.on()
        self._projector.wide_screen_mode()
        self._amplifier.on()
        self._amplifier.set_source("BluRay")
        self._amplifier.set_volume(5)
        self._bluray.on()
        self._bluray.play(movie_title)

screens.title: Facade — HomeTheater Python demo
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through the home theater example to see how a facade orchestrates multiple devices. The subsystem classes each provide small behaviors: the projector can be turned on, set to wide screen mode, or turned off; the amplifier can set source and volume; the player can play or stop media; and lights can dim or brighten. The HomeTheaterFacade constructor receives instances of these subsystem classes and stores them. When the client calls watch movie, the facade calls lights. dim to set the mood, powers on the projector and sets widescreen, powers on and configures the amplifier, then powers and tells the player to start. For ending the movie, the facade sequences stop and off calls in the appropriate order. This pattern reduces the client's code to two simple calls. A common misstep is writing a facade that replicates subsystem functionality or exposes every subsystem method directly through the facade; that sacrifices the simplification goal. Instead, choose a small set of cohesive operations that reflect client tasks, and keep the facade thin — orchestration only. When testing, verify both the subsystems independently and the facade for correct sequencing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Facade Code
Subsystem classes and facade orchestration
class Projector:
    def on(self): print("Projector: ON")
    def off(self): print("Projector: OFF")
    def wide_screen_mode(self): print("Projector: Wide screen mode enabled")

class Amplifier:
    def on(self): print("Amplifier: ON")
    def off(self): print("Amplifier: OFF")
    def set_volume(self, level): print(f"Amplifier: Volume set to {level}")
    def set_source(self, source): print(f"Amplifier: Source set to {source}")

class BluRayPlayer:
    def on(self): print("BluRayPlayer: ON")
    def off(self): print("BluRayPlayer: OFF")
    def play(self, movie): print(f"BluRayPlayer: Playing '{movie}'")
Facade implementation
class HomeTheaterFacade:
    def __init__(self, projector, amplifier, bluray, lights):
        self._projector = projector
        self._amplifier = amplifier
        self._bluray = bluray
        self._lights = lights

    def watch_movie(self, movie_title):
        self._lights.dim(10)
        self._projector.on()
        self._projector.wide_screen_mode()
        self._amplifier.on()
        self._amplifier.set_source("BluRay")
        self._amplifier.set_volume(5)
        self._bluray.on()
        self._bluray.play(movie_title)

    def end_movie(self):
        self._bluray.stop()
        self._bluray.off()
        self._amplifier.off()
        self._projector.off()
        self._lights.brighten()
Test scenario
Instantiate subsystems, create the facade, call watch_movie, observe printed device actions, then call end_movie to check shutdown order.
Common Mistake
Avoid exposing every subsystem method through the facade — prefer a small set of high‑level operations.
Key Takeaway

The facade simplifies client code by orchestrating subsystems, but subsystems remain independently testable.

screens.title: Composite operations — add, remove, traverse
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding how composites manage children and propagate operations clarifies runtime behavior and helps avoid bugs. The usual composite process begins with construction: composites start with an empty child list. Developers call add to attach leaves or other composites; remove detaches a child. For traversal operations like display, the composite calls its own display behavior and then iterates over children calling their display with increased indentation. For aggregation operations like get_size, it initializes an accumulator, calls get_size on each child, and sums the results. In practice, ensure that add and remove are only on composites; leaves should not implement meaningless management methods. A helpful example: create a root directory, add two files and a subdirectory; add files to the subdirectory and call display — the output should show nested entries with indentation. A frequent error is accidental circular references when moving nodes between parents without removing them from the old parent. To avoid this, implement clear ownership semantics or remove from old parent before adding to a new one. Finally, consider iteration order if ordering matters, and design methods to be exception-safe to keep tree state consistent.

keyIdea.title: Operation sequence
keyIdea.text: Composites manage children with add/remove and propagate display/get_size calls recursively, aggregating results without client type checks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Composite Operations
Typical operation sequence
1. Create
Initialize composites with empty children lists and leaves with their data.
2. Add/Remove
Attach and detach children via composite-only methods to maintain invariants.
3. Traverse
Call operations that recurse through children and aggregate or format results.
Example run
root = Directory("root")

screens.title: Facade vs Adapter vs Decorator
screens.narratorSegment: Structural patterns sometimes overlap in appearance, so it's important to know their distinct intent. Facade provides a simplified A P I for a subsystem by aggregating many interfaces into a small set of higher‑level methods. Adapter converts one interface into another so that an existing class can be used where a different interface is expected; it focuses on interface compatibility, not on simplifying multiple classes. Decorator adds responsibilities to a single object dynamically, wrapping it so it appears to the client as the same type but with extra behavior. A practical way to choose: if you need to treat composite objects uniformly, use Composite; if you need a single convenient entry point to many classes, use Facade; if you must change the interface of an object to fit a client, use Adapter; if you need to add features to one object instance without subclassing, use Decorator. A common mistake is selecting Facade when the real need is to adapt incompatible interfaces, which leads to a facade that merely translates rather than simplifying. Keep intent front and center when selecting a pattern.

screens.title: Design rules and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: As you apply Composite and Facade, follow a few practical rules to keep designs maintainable. First, keep the Component interface small and focused on truly shared operations like display, render, or compute aggregate values. Second, place child management methods such as add and remove on Composite only; avoid forcing leaves to provide no‑op implementations. Third, design facades for meaningful workflows — name methods after client tasks and keep orchestration logic centralized. Fourth, do not hide everything behind a facade; allow clients to access subsystem classes for advanced or specialized behaviors. Fifth, test subsystems independently and test facades for correct sequencing. Watch out for anti‑patterns: interface bloat in Component, facades that duplicate business logic, and circular references when reparenting nodes. Finally, document ownership semantics and lifetime expectations to avoid memory leaks or dangling references. Following these rules keeps your software modular and easier to reason about, while both patterns together let you reduce duplication and create clear boundaries between structure and orchestration. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll study two complementary structural patterns that help you manage complexity in software. First, you will learn the Composite pattern, which lets you represent part‑whole hierarchies so clients call the same operations on single objects and on object collections. Think of files and directories: the same display or size calculation works whether you call it on a single file or on an entire directory tree. Second, you'll learn the Facade pattern, which creates a single, higher‑level interface to orchestrate many subsystem classes so a client performs a complex task with a single call. For example, a watch movie method can dim lights, start the projector, and set the amplifier without the client wiring all those calls together. Together these patterns let you reduce duplication, simplify client code, and keep subsystems decoupled. We'll walk concrete Python examples for each, point out common pitfalls such as bloated interfaces or hiding too much, and finish with a practical activity. Consider what large system you interact with daily that feels awkward to use; this lesson will give you two design tools to fix it.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about and implement two structural patterns that tame complexity. First, you will understand how to design a Component interface and separate Leaf and Composite implementations so that client code calls the same operations on a single object or an entire tree. You will practice this by modeling file system entries or organizational charts, implementing display and size calculations that recurse through children. Second, you will be able to design a Facade that hides complex orchestration behind a concise A P I. You will implement a home‑theater or DevOps pipeline facade that sequences multiple subsystem calls, and you will learn when a facade should expose or hide subsystem classes. Finally, you will learn to recognize pitfalls: do not put methods in the Component that only make sense for one role, and do not let a facade become a god object that duplicates subsystem functionality. These skills help you build modular, maintainable systems that are easier to test and adapt.

These objectives focus on practical skills and common pitfalls. You will implement Composite tree structures with working add and remove operations and a display behavior that recurses cleanly. Practice computing aggregated values like total size, and pay attention to interface design: only put methods in the shared Component interface that make sense for both leaves and composites. You will also implement a Facade that orchestrates multiple subsystem classes and exposes high‑level operations, such as watch or run pipeline. While writing facades, make clear decisions about which subsystem functionality to expose and when to allow clients to access the subsystem directly. A frequent mistake is making the facade do too much or, conversely, exposing every subsystem method again through the facade, which defeats simplification. By the end of the exercises you should be able to choose between exposing a facade, delegating specific calls, or leaving fine‑grained control to advanced clients.

Let's contrast the two patterns by focusing on intent and client impact. The Composite pattern addresses the problem of uniformity: you want clients to treat single objects and recursive compositions the same way. The core of Composite is a shared Component interface plus leaf and composite implementations; common operations are implemented at both levels and composites delegate to their children. Use Composite when you have part‑whole hierarchies such as file systems, UI element trees, or organizational charts. A common misconception is that Composite is about simplifying subsystem complexity; instead, it focuses on uniformity of structure and recursion. Facade solves a different problem: an application must interact with a set of heterogeneous subsystem classes, and that interaction is complex. The Facade provides a higher‑level A P I that orchestrates subsystem calls. For example, a watch movie method sequences lights, projector, and player. A misconception is to confuse Facade with Adapter: an Adapter changes a single interface to match another, while Facade offers a new, simplified A P I that aggregates many interfaces. Finally, Decorator is sometimes confused with Composite; Decorator adds behavior to single objects, not to whole trees. Decide by asking: does the problem require uniform object composition or simplified orchestration of many classes?

The Composite pattern models part‑whole hierarchies by defining three roles. First, the Component is an abstract interface or base class that declares the operations common to both individual items and compositions. Keep this interface minimal — include only methods that make sense for both leaves and composites. Second, the Leaf is a concrete object with no children that implements the Component interface. Leaves provide the fundamental behavior, like returning their own size or rendering themselves. Third, the Composite is a container that also implements Component and manages child components with add, remove, and get_children methods. When a composite receives an operation like display or get_size, it forwards that call to each child and aggregates the results. A concrete example is a directory: a directory lists itself and then iterates through children to display their entries; size is computed by summing child sizes. A common mistake is adding management or traversal-specific methods to Component that only composites need. Instead, place child management on Composite itself and keep the Component contract focused on shared operations. Understanding these roles helps you design clear, testable hierarchies.

Now we'll walk through a Python implementation that shows the Composite pattern in action. The example defines a FileSystemComponent base class with display and get_size methods. The File leaf stores its own size and prints its name and size when asked to display. The Directory composite keeps a list of children and implements add and remove. When display is called on a directory, it prints its heading and then calls display on each child, increasing the indentation. For get_size, the directory iterates through children and sums their sizes, returning the aggregate. A practical example: if you call get_size on the root directory, it returns the total of nested files even if they are many levels deep. Watch for an important design decision: child management methods are on Directory, not on File or the base component. A common learner mistake is to include traversal helpers in the base interface, which forces leaves to implement meaningless behavior. When testing, create a nested structure with files and directories, call display to verify formatting, and call get_size to confirm the sum. This demonstrates the recursive power of Composite and why clients can use a single interface for both leaves and compositions.

The Facade pattern provides a single, higher‑level interface to a collection of subsystem classes so clients can complete a common task without coordinating many low‑level calls. The Facade encapsulates the orchestration logic and delegates work to subsystem classes internally. The facade itself should not contain the core subsystem behavior; it directs where work is done. For example, a home theater facade might call lights, projector, amplifier, and player methods in sequence when asked to watch a movie. This hides the orchestration details and reduces coupling between the client and the subsystem. Remember that a facade is an optional convenience; clients that need fine‑grained control can still access subsystem classes directly. A common misconception is that a facade replaces unit testing for subsystem classes; you still test subsystems individually and test the facade for orchestration. Use facades to reduce repetitive wiring code and to provide a stable entry point to a changing subsystem implementation. Facade Pattern — Intent and structure means facade orchestrates multiple classes to provide a simple api for common client tasks while keeping subsystems testable and accessible.. In practical terms, simplify client interaction with a complex subsystem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's step through the home theater example to see how a facade orchestrates multiple devices. The subsystem classes each provide small behaviors: the projector can be turned on, set to wide screen mode, or turned off; the amplifier can set source and volume; the player can play or stop media; and lights can dim or brighten. The HomeTheaterFacade constructor receives instances of these subsystem classes and stores them. When the client calls watch movie, the facade calls lights. dim to set the mood, powers on the projector and sets widescreen, powers on and configures the amplifier, then powers and tells the player to start. For ending the movie, the facade sequences stop and off calls in the appropriate order. This pattern reduces the client's code to two simple calls. A common misstep is writing a facade that replicates subsystem functionality or exposes every subsystem method directly through the facade; that sacrifices the simplification goal. Instead, choose a small set of cohesive operations that reflect client tasks, and keep the facade thin — orchestration only. When testing, verify both the subsystems independently and the facade for correct sequencing.

Understanding how composites manage children and propagate operations clarifies runtime behavior and helps avoid bugs. The usual composite process begins with construction: composites start with an empty child list. Developers call add to attach leaves or other composites; remove detaches a child. For traversal operations like display, the composite calls its own display behavior and then iterates over children calling their display with increased indentation. For aggregation operations like get_size, it initializes an accumulator, calls get_size on each child, and sums the results. In practice, ensure that add and remove are only on composites; leaves should not implement meaningless management methods. A helpful example: create a root directory, add two files and a subdirectory; add files to the subdirectory and call display — the output should show nested entries with indentation. A frequent error is accidental circular references when moving nodes between parents without removing them from the old parent. To avoid this, implement clear ownership semantics or remove from old parent before adding to a new one. Finally, consider iteration order if ordering matters, and design methods to be exception-safe to keep tree state consistent.
